text: Every file on Linux has an owner, a group, and a permission string that decides who can read it, write it, or run it. This lesson covers how to create users and groups, how to read and set those permissions as both letters and numbers, and why root and sudo exist in the first place.

useradd creates a new account — the -m flag creates their home directory, -s sets their default shell. passwd sets their password. groupadd creates a group, and usermod -aG adds an existing user to it — the -a matters, because leaving it off silently removes them from every other group they were in.

Permissions come in three triplets of r, w, and x — read, write, execute — for the owner, the group, and everyone else. Each letter has a numeric value: read is 4, write is 2, execute is 1, added together. chmod 755 sets owner to rwx, group to r-x, and other to r-x — the permission set you'll see on almost every script and web file on a real server.

ls -l deploy.sh shows the full permission string next to the file, right alongside its owner and group. chmod changes those bits, either as an octal number like 755 or symbolically, like chmod u plus x to add execute for the owner alone without touching group or other at all.

chown user colon group file changes both who owns a file and which group owns it — and those are exactly the two columns the rwx triplets get checked against. Ownership and permissions work together, not separately.

Root is Linux's superuser, bypassing every permission check, which is exactly why staying logged in as root all the time is dangerous. sudo lets an authorized user run one command as root at a time, after re-entering their own password, with the action logged — which is why production servers almost never allow a direct root login. Next up: package management, and installing software the right way across distro families.
